'''Janet Marie Conrad''' (born 1963) is an American experimental [[physicist]], researcher, and professor at [[MIT]] studying [[elementary particle physics]]. Her work focuses on [[neutrino]] properties and the techniques for studying them. In recognition of her efforts, Conrad has been the recipient of several highly prestigious awards during her career, including an [[Sloan Research Fellowship|Alfred P. Sloan Research Fellow]], a [[Guggenheim Fellowship|Guggenheim Fellow]], and the [[American Physical Society]] [[Maria Goeppert-Mayer Award]].

==Education==
Conrad obtained a physics B.A. from [[Swarthmore College]] in 1985. She then went to [[Oxford University]] to complete a M.Sc. in High Energy Physics as a member of the [[European Muon Collaboration]] in 1987 then to [[Harvard University]] to complete a PhD in High Energy Physics in 1993.<ref name="MIT_CV">{{cite web|url=http://www2.lns.mit.edu/~conrad/cv2016.pdf|publisher=MIT|title=cv2016.pdf|access-date=25 April 2018}}</ref>

==Career==
Following Conrad's sophomore year at Swarthmore, she spent her summer in [[Cambridge, Massachusetts]] working with Francis Pipkin at Harvard, at her uncle's suggestion.<ref name="new_yorker"/> 
The following summer, Conrad worked with him at [[Fermilab]].<ref name="new_yorker"/>

After graduating from Harvard in 1993, Conrad took a position as a postdoctoral research associate at the [[Nevis Laboratories]], operated by [[Columbia University]]. 
In 1995, she joined Columbia's physics department as an assistant professor. 
In 1996 she was awarded the DOE Outstanding Junior Investigator Award for a study entitled ''Construction of a Decay Channel for the NuTeV Experiment at Fermilab''
.<ref name="DOE_OJI">{{cite web|title=DOE OUTSTANDING JUNIOR INVESTIGATOR PROGRAM AWARDEES|url=https://science.energy.gov/~/media/hep/pdf/files/pdfs/OJI_ALL_Awards.pdf|website=DOE Office of Science|access-date=26 April 2018}}</ref> 
She gained [[academic tenure|tenure]] at Columbia in 1999.
In 2002, she was nominated by the [[American Physical Society]]'s Division of Particles and Fields for fellowship with the APS, citing "her leadership in experimental neutrino physics, particularly for initiating and leading the NuTeV decay channel experiment and the Mini-BooNe neutrino oscillations experiment".<ref name="aps_fellow">{{cite web|title=APS Fellow Archive|url=https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/fellowships/archive-all.cfm?initial=&year=2002&unit_id=DPF&institution=Columbia+University|publisher=American Physical Society|access-date=27 April 2018}}</ref> 
From 2005 until 2008, Conrad was a Columbia Distinguished Faculty Fellow, and was promoted to the [[Financial endowment#Endowed professorships|endowed position]] of Walter O. Lecroy Professor in 2006.<ref name="MIT_CV"/> 
In 2008, Conrad left Columbia to join [[MIT]]'s physics department as a professor.<ref name="MIT_CV"/>

Conrad is a member of several physics collaborations, including [[MicroBooNE]], DAEδALUS, Short-Baseline Near Detector ([[SBND]]), and [[IceCube Neutrino Observatory|IceCube]]. 
She was previously a member of 
[[Double Chooz]] (2006-2014),
[[SciBooNE]] (2005-2011),
[[MiniBooNE]] (1997-2014),
CCFR/NuTeV (1993-2001),
E665 (1984-1996), and
[[European Muon Collaboration|EMC]] (1985-1986).<ref name="MIT_CV"/>

In addition, she has acted as a spokesperson for IsoDAR/DAEdALUS
<ref>{{cite web|title=Janet Conrad|url=https://www.psfc.mit.edu/people/faculty/janet-conrad|website=Plasma Science and Fusion Center|publisher=Massachusetts Institute of Technology|access-date=26 April 2018}}</ref>
and MiniBooNE,<ref name="MIT_CV"/> of which she was a founding member.<ref name="guggenheim"/>

==Other==
In 2012, Conrad took part in a panel with the World Science Festival, speaking to the public about neutrinos.<ref>{{cite web|title=What Do Neutrino Oscillations Tell Us?|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lSUQFPuDvOA|website=YouTube| date=21 November 2014 |publisher=World Science Festival|access-date=26 April 2018}}</ref>

Inspired by detector development efforts while working on IceCube,<ref>{{cite web|title=CosmicWatch|url=http://www.cosmicwatch.lns.mit.edu/|access-date=26 April 2018}}</ref> Conrad took part in the development of a low-cost tabletop [[muon]] detector.<ref>{{cite news|title=The $100 muon detector|url=https://www.symmetrymagazine.org/article/the-100-muon-detector|access-date=26 April 2018|date=19 August 2016}}</ref>

In 2015, Conrad and fellow MIT professor [[Lindley Winslow]] were consulted as experts in the culture and science of physics for the 2016 film ''[[Ghostbusters (2016 film)|Ghostbusters]]''.<ref>{{cite web|title=Ghostbusters: Yes, the Equations are Correct|url=http://scienceandfilm.org/articles/2734/ghostbusters-yes-the-equations-are-correct|website=Sloan Science and Film}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=The MIT Physicists Who Infused Ghostbusters With Real Science|url=https://www.wired.com/2016/07/ghostbusters-mit-physicists/|access-date=26 April 2018|publisher=Wired}}</ref>

==Personal life==
Janet Conrad was born October 23, 1963, in [[Wooster, Ohio]].<ref name="MIT_CV"/> 
She was a member of [[4-H]] as a child in Ohio.<ref name="new_yorker">{{cite magazine|title=Fun With Physics|url=https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2003/06/02/fun-with-physics|access-date=26 April 2018|magazine=The New Yorker|date=2 June 2003}}</ref>

Conrad is the niece of chemistry Nobel Laureate [[William Lipscomb]].<ref name="new_yorker"/>

Conrad is married to fellow physicist Vassili Papavassiliou,<ref name="new_yorker"/> a professor at [[New Mexico State University]]<ref>{{cite web|title=Vassili Papavassiliou|url=http://physics.nmsu.edu/people/facstaff/VassiliPapavassiliou.html|website=New Mexico State University|access-date=26 April 2018|archive-date=18 October 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181018171804/http://physics.nmsu.edu/people/facstaff/VassiliPapavassiliou.html|url-status=dead}}</ref>
